explain.say: Before any building in Lagos or Jakarta goes up, someone drills a borehole and asks: what is this ground made of? Engineers sort soil grains by size into gravel, sand, silt and clay. On the board is a typical profile. Let us read it from the top down.

explain.say: Gravel and sand are coarse soils: you can see the grains. Their sizes are found by sieving, shaking the soil through finer and finer meshes. In the Indian and Unified systems, sand runs from zero point zero seven five to four point seven five millimetres, and gravel is bigger. They get their strength from grains rubbing on each other. Why do you think they drain so fast?

explain.say: Big gaps between big grains! Below zero point zero seven five millimetres come the fines, silt and clay, too small for sieves. Clay grains are tiny flat plates under two thousandths of a millimetre. Clay holds water, turns sticky and plastic when wet, and shrinks and swells. India's black cotton soils crack open in summer and heave in the monsoon.

explain.say: To tell silt from clay we use the Atterberg limits, the water contents where soil turns from crumbly to plastic to liquid. Plot plasticity index against liquid limit: above the A-line is clay, below it silt. A sample with liquid limit fifty and plasticity index thirty sits above the line, which reads twenty one point nine there. So it is a high plasticity clay.

explain.say: Put it together and every soil gets a short name, like SW for well-graded sand or CH for high plasticity clay. Peat and organic soils get flagged, because they squash a great deal. Well done! Challenge: a soil has a liquid limit of forty and a plasticity index of ten. Silt or clay?

faq.q: What are the size limits of gravel, sand, silt and clay?
faq.a: In the Indian and Unified systems, gravel is 4.75 to 75 millimetres and sand 0.075 to 4.75 millimetres. Finer than 0.075 millimetres are silt and clay, with clay-size particles under 0.002 millimetres. British practice uses slightly different limits.
asks: How big is a sand grain?

faq.q: How do you tell silt from clay?
faq.a: Use the plasticity chart. Plot plasticity index against liquid limit: points above the A-line are clays, below it silts. In the field, clay feels sticky and can be rolled into thin threads; silt feels smooth and crumbles.

They are water contents where a fine soil changes state: the plastic limit, where it stops crumbling and becomes mouldable, and the liquid limit, where it starts to flow. Their difference is the plasticity index.
asks: What is liquid limit and plastic limit?

faq.q: Why are clay soils a problem for foundations?
faq.a: Clays compress slowly under load, causing long-term settlement, and some swell when wet and shrink when dry, cracking buildings. They also lose strength when soaked.
A sieve analysis shakes a dried soil sample through a stack of sieves with smaller and smaller openings and weighs what stays on each. It gives the grading curve of coarse soils.
asks: How do you do a grain size analysis?

facts: In the Unified and Indian soil classification systems, sand ranges from 0.075 to 4.75 mm.
The A-line on Casagrande's plasticity chart is PI = 0.73(LL − 20).
The Atterberg limits are named after the Swedish scientist Albert Atterberg.

quiz.say: A fine soil has a liquid limit of 60 and a plasticity index of 20. Using the A-line, is it silt or clay?
quiz.show: A fine soil has LL = 60 and PI = 20. With the A-line PI = 0.73(LL − 20), is it silt or clay?
quiz.why: The A-line at 60 is 0.73 × 40 = 29.2. A PI of 20 is below it, so silt, and LL over 50 means high plasticity.

wrong.0: Clay would need a PI above 29.2 at this liquid limit.
wrong.2: A soil with a liquid limit and plasticity is fine-grained, not sand.
